explanation:
## The pairings

| Collective | Movement |
| --- | --- |
| `MPI_Bcast` | one to all, same data |
| `MPI_Scatter` | one to all, split |
| `MPI_Gather` | all to one, assembled |
| `MPI_Allreduce` | all to all, combined |
| `MPI_Barrier` | no data, just synchronisation |

The leftover is **`MPI_Alltoall`**, where every rank sends something different to every other rank. With `P` ranks it moves `P^2` messages and is the collective that stops a program scaling — it is the communication pattern of a distributed transpose, and of the shuffle stage of a distributed FFT or sort.

## The distinctions that matter

**Bcast against Scatter.** Both go from one rank to all, and the difference is whether the data is replicated or divided. Bcast gives everyone the same `n` elements; Scatter gives each of `P` ranks a different `n/P` elements. Using Bcast where you meant Scatter is a correctness bug that looks like a performance bug: everything runs and every rank redundantly processes the whole array.

**Gather against Reduce.** Both go from all to one. Gather *concatenates* — rank 0 ends up with `P` pieces laid end to end. Reduce *combines* with an operator — rank 0 ends up with one value. If you find yourself gathering an array and then summing it on rank 0, you wanted a reduce, and the reduce is both shorter and much faster.

**Reduce against Allreduce.** Identical except for where the answer lands: Reduce leaves it on one root, Allreduce leaves it on everyone. Allreduce is roughly a reduce followed by a broadcast and costs about twice a reduce — so if only the root needs it, do not ask for Allreduce out of habit. The reverse mistake is worse though: a `Reduce` followed by a hand-written `Bcast` is slower than `Allreduce`, because the library can fuse them.

**Barrier.** Moves nothing and is still a collective, because every rank must call it. It is also the one most often used unnecessarily: MPI's collectives already synchronise as much as their semantics require, so a Barrier before a Bcast adds latency and no safety. The honest uses are timing a phase and ordering output.

## Costs, which is the practical knowledge

With `P` ranks and `n` bytes, on a good implementation:

| Collective | Latency | Bandwidth term |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Bcast | `O(log P)` | `O(n)` |
| Scatter / Gather | `O(log P)` | `O(n)` |
| Allreduce | `O(log P)` | `O(n)` |
| Barrier | `O(log P)` | — |
| **Alltoall** | `O(P)` | `O(nP)` |

The important line is the last one. Everything else is logarithmic in the number of ranks; Alltoall is linear, and its data volume grows with `P` too. A code that scales nicely to 100 ranks and falls over at 10,000 usually has an Alltoall in it.

The `O(log P)` figures are not free either — they come from the implementations being clever. Bcast is a tree, not a loop of sends. Allreduce on large buffers is usually **reduce-scatter followed by allgather** (the "ring allreduce"), which achieves bandwidth-optimal `2n(P-1)/P` bytes per rank instead of the naive `nP`. That algorithm is the reason distributed deep-learning training works at all: synchronising gradients every step is an allreduce of hundreds of megabytes, and NCCL is essentially a very good ring allreduce.

## Why to use the collective rather than writing it

It is tempting to write a loop of `MPI_Send` and claim it is the same thing. It is not: the library picks an algorithm based on message size, rank count and the actual network topology, uses shared memory between ranks on the same node, and may offload the reduction to the network switch. A hand-rolled Bcast is typically several times slower at scale and never improves when you move to better hardware.
